config.title: Generic List<T>

intro.title: Generic List<T>
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a reusable List<T> component in React with TypeScript that can display any type of data, such as a list of strings or numbers. You'll learn how to use TypeScript generics to create flexible components that maintain type safety, ensuring your code is both adaptable and reliable. The main technologies involved are React for the UI structure and TypeScript's generic type parameters to define the component's prop types. By the end, you'll understand how to write a single component that works with multiple data types while getting full IntelliSense support and compile-time error checking.
intro.usecase: Generic List<T> components are foundational in building reusable, type-safe UI elements across modern applications. For example, a dashboard might use a generic list to display a collection of user cards, product items, or notification alerts, where the item type changes but the rendering logic remains consistent. Similarly, a data table component can leverage generics to handle rows of different data structures—like sales orders or inventory items—while maintaining strict type checking in TypeScript. This pattern allows developers to write a single, flexible component instead of duplicating code for each data type, enhancing maintainability and reducing bugs in complex interfaces like admin panels or content feeds.

objectives: Implement a generic List<T> component that accepts a type parameter
Configure the List<T> component to render items of any specified type
Initialize and manipulate state within a generic component using TypeScript
Apply type constraints to ensure the generic component handles specific data structures
Construct a reusable generic component that maintains type safety throughout the application
Integrate the generic List<T> component with different data types in a React application
Render type-safe lists by passing appropriate props to the generic component

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing modules
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create a generic List component with type parameter T
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named List that accepts a generic type parameter T. Define its props interface to include an items array of type T[].
steps.hint: Start with 'function List<T>' or 'const List = <T>'. Then define an interface for props containing items: T[].
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your generic List component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic List component with type parameter T and props interface defined.
successCriteria: List component is defined with generic type parameter T and props interface containing items: T[].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your List component accepts a generic type parameter T and has a props interface with items: T[].
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't match requirements. It should be a generic component named List with type parameter T and props containing items array.

steps.title: Define props interface for List<T>
steps.instruction: Define an interface named ListProps<T> with two properties: items of type T[] and renderItem of type (item: T) => React.ReactNode.
steps.hint: Create a TypeScript interface with a generic type parameter T. The items property should be an array of T, and renderItem should be a function that takes a T and returns React content.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ListProps<T> interface is defined with the correct property types, ready to be used as the props type for the List component.
successCriteria: ListProps<T> interface exists with items: T[] and renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that both properties (items and renderItem) have the correct types as specified.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to define ListProps<T> with the required properties and types.

steps.title: Implement the List component structure
steps.instruction: Implement the List component function that accepts ListProps<T> and returns JSX. Use the generic type parameter T in the function signature and return a simple wrapper element.
steps.hint: Create a function component named List that takes props of type ListProps<T>. Return a <div> element for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: The List component function is implemented with the correct generic type parameter and returns a JSX element.
successCriteria: List component function is defined with generic type parameter T, accepts ListProps<T>, and returns JSX (a <div> element).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the List component accepts ListProps<T> and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The List component implementation is missing or incorrect. Check the function signature and return statement.

steps.title: Add state to manage selected item
steps.instruction: Inside your List component, initialize a state variable called 'selectedItem' with type T | null using useState. Set its initial value to null.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the generic type parameter for useState as T | null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: useState with a generic type
const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The List component will have a selectedItem state variable that can store either an item of type T or null.
successCriteria: selectedItem state is initialized with useState<T | null>(null) inside the List component
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've used useState with the correct type annotation (T | null) and initial value (null).
steps.feedbackWrong: The selectedItem state wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use useState with the generic type T | null and initial value null.

steps.title: Create handler to select an item
steps.instruction: Inside the List component, create a function named handleSelect that takes a parameter 'item' of type T and updates the selectedItem state with that item.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts an item parameter and calls setSelectedItem with it. Remember to use the generic type T for the parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The List component will have a handleSelect function that can update the selectedItem state when called with an item of type T.
successCriteria: A function named handleSelect is defined inside the List component, it accepts a parameter of type T, and calls setSelectedItem with that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your handleSelect function accepts a parameter of type T and calls setSelectedItem with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSelect function should be defined inside the List component, accept a parameter of type T, and update the selectedItem state.

steps.title: Render the list items using renderItem prop
steps.instruction: Inside the List component, map through the items array and render each item using the renderItem prop function.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the items array. For each item, call renderItem(item) to get the React node to display.
steps.expectedOutcome: The List component will render each item from the items array using the renderItem function passed as a prop.
successCriteria: The items array is mapped, and each item is rendered by calling renderItem(item) inside a list item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling renderItem(item) for each item in the map function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The list items are not being rendered using the renderItem prop. Check that you're mapping through items and calling renderItem for each item.

steps.title: Add click handlers to list items
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to each list item that calls handleSelect with the current item.
steps.hint: Use onClick={() => handleSelect(item)} on the <li> element.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each list item will be clickable and will trigger the selection handler when clicked.
successCriteria: The onClick handler is added to each <li> element and calls handleSelect with the current item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an onClick handler, but make sure it calls handleSelect with the current item.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding onClick={() => handleSelect(item)} to each <li> element.

steps.title: Display selected item information
steps.instruction: Add a conditional section below the list to display the selected item when it exists. Use a ternary operator to show a paragraph with the text 'Selected: ' followed by the selected item's rendered content, or null if no item is selected.
steps.hint:
You can place this after the closing tag. Use selectedItem ?

Selected: {renderItem(selectedItem)}

: null.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show a paragraph with the selected item's rendered content below the list when an item is selected, and nothing when no item is selected.
successCriteria: A ternary operator conditionally renders a paragraph with 'Selected: ' followed by renderItem(selectedItem) when selectedItem exists, otherwise renders null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your conditional rendering. Make sure you're using selectedItem ? ... : null and displaying 'Selected: ' followed by the rendered content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The selected item isn't being displayed conditionally. Review how to use ternary operators in JSX to show content only when selectedItem has a value.

steps.title: Use the List component with specific types
steps.instruction: Create a new component named App that uses the List component with a specific type (e.g., string or number) and provides appropriate data and renderItem function.
steps.hint: Instantiate the generic List component with a concrete type by passing items and renderItem props. For example, use an array of strings and a renderItem function that returns each string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component should render a List component with a concrete type (e.g., string or number), passing items and renderItem props that match that type.
successCriteria: App component is created, List component is instantiated with a concrete type, items array and renderItem function are provided with correct types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your App component uses the List component with a concrete type (e.g., <List<string>>) and provides both items and renderItem props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should use the List component with a specific type. Check that you're passing items and renderItem props with matching types.
